title: MATH GAOKAO - 17
description: Authentic-style mathematics problems inspired by China’s Gaokao — build deeper understanding, sharper thinking, and real exam readiness.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the sufficient condition in an implication.
questions.question: Consider the statement “If \(x>2\), then \(x^2>4\).” Which statement is true?
questions.explanation: In an implication \(p\rightarrow q\), the condition \(p\) is sufficient for \(q\). Here \(p\) is \(x>2\) and \(q\) is \(x^2>4\). Therefore, \(x>2\) is sufficient for \(x^2>4\). Option A is false because \(x^2>4\) does not imply \(x>2\); for example, \(x=-3\) gives \(x^2=9>4\), but \(x>2\) is false.
questions.hint: In \(p\rightarrow q\), the hypothesis \(p\) is the sufficient condition for \(q\).

questions.learningObjective: Identify the necessary condition in an implication.
questions.question: Consider the statement “If \(n\) is divisible by \(6\), then \(n\) is divisible by \(3\).” Which condition is necessary for \(n\) to be divisible by \(6\)?
questions.explanation: In an implication \(p\rightarrow q\), the conclusion \(q\) is necessary for \(p\). Here \(p\) is “\(n\) is divisible by \(6\)” and \(q\) is “\(n\) is divisible by \(3\).” Therefore, divisibility by \(3\) is necessary for divisibility by \(6\). Divisibility by \(6\) is sufficient but not necessary, since \(3\) is divisible by \(3\) but not by \(6\).
questions.hint: In \(p\rightarrow q\), the conclusion \(q\) is the necessary condition for \(p\).

questions.concept: Necessary and Sufficient Conditions in Geometry
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a geometric implication in terms of necessary and sufficient conditions.
questions.question: Consider the statement “If a quadrilateral is a square, then it is a rectangle.” Which statement is true?

options.label: A
options.text: Being a rectangle is necessary for being a square.

options.label: B
options.text: Being a rectangle is sufficient for being a square.

questions.explanation: The statement has the form \(p\rightarrow q\), where \(p\) is “a quadrilateral is a square” and \(q\) is “it is a rectangle.” In \(p\rightarrow q\), \(q\) is necessary for \(p\). Therefore, being a rectangle is necessary for being a square. Option B is false because a rectangle is not necessarily a square.
questions.hint: In \(p\rightarrow q\), the conclusion \(q\) is necessary for \(p\).

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a sufficient condition from a necessary condition.
questions.question: For real numbers \(x\), consider the condition \(x=2\). Which statement is true?
questions.explanation: If \(x=2\), then \(x^2=4\), so \(x=2\) is sufficient for \(x^2=4\). However, \(x=2\) is not necessary because \(x=-2\) also gives \(x^2=4\). Therefore, the true statement is that \(x=2\) is sufficient for \(x^2=4\).
questions.hint: Check whether the condition guarantees the conclusion, and whether the conclusion can occur without it.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret differentiability and continuity in terms of sufficient conditions.
questions.question: Consider the statement “If a function is differentiable at a point, then it is continuous there.” Which statement is true?
questions.explanation: The implication states that differentiability at a point implies continuity there. Therefore, differentiability is sufficient for continuity. It is not necessary, because a function can be continuous without being differentiable; for example, \(f(x)=|x|\) is continuous at \(0\) but not differentiable at \(0\).
questions.hint: The hypothesis of an implication is the sufficient condition.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a necessary condition that is not sufficient.
questions.question: Consider the statement “If \(n\) is divisible by \(4\), then \(n\) is even.” Which statement is true?

options.label: A
options.text: Being even is necessary for being divisible by \(4\).

options.label: B
options.text: Being even is sufficient for being divisible by \(4\).

questions.explanation: The implication “divisible by \(4\) \(\rightarrow\) even” shows that being even is necessary for being divisible by \(4\). It is not sufficient, because \(2\) is even but not divisible by \(4\). Therefore, option A is true and option B is false.
questions.hint: In \(p\rightarrow q\), the conclusion \(q\) is necessary for \(p\).

questions.learningObjective: Determine which statement about sufficient conditions is false.
questions.question: Consider the conditions \(x>3\) and \(x>1\). Which statement is false?
questions.explanation: If \(x>3\), then certainly \(x>1\), so \(x>3\) is sufficient for \(x>1\). Thus A is true. However, \(x>1\) does not guarantee \(x>3\); for example, \(x=2\) satisfies \(x>1\) but not \(x>3\). Therefore, B is false.
questions.hint: Test whether the hypothesis guarantees the conclusion in each option.

questions.learningObjective: Determine which condition is sufficient for another in an equation context.
questions.question: For real numbers \(x\), consider the conditions \(P\): \(x^2=1\) and \(Q\): \(x=1\). Which statement is true?
questions.explanation: If \(x=1\), then \(x^2=1\), so \(Q\) is sufficient for \(P\). However, \(x^2=1\) does not imply \(x=1\), because \(x=-1\) also satisfies \(x^2=1\). Therefore, \(P\) is not sufficient for \(Q\), and the true statement is option B.
questions.hint: Check whether each condition guarantees the other, and look for counterexamples.

questions.concept: Necessary but Not Sufficient Condition in Divisibility
questions.learningObjective: Interpret divisibility conditions in terms of necessary and sufficient conditions.
questions.question: For integers \(n\), which statement is true?

options.label: A
options.text: Divisibility by \(3\) is necessary but not sufficient for divisibility by \(9\).

options.label: B
options.text: Divisibility by \(3\) is sufficient but not necessary for divisibility by \(9\).

questions.explanation: If \(n\) is divisible by \(9\), then \(n\) is divisible by \(3\). Therefore, divisibility by \(3\) is necessary for divisibility by \(9\). However, divisibility by \(3\) is not sufficient, because \(n=3\) is divisible by \(3\) but not by \(9\). Hence option A is true and option B is false.
questions.hint: Use the implication “divisible by \(9\) \(\rightarrow\) divisible by \(3\).”

questions.learningObjective: Determine which inequality condition is sufficient for another.
questions.question: For real numbers \(x\), consider the conditions \(P\): \(x>0\) and \(Q\): \(x^2>0\). Which statement is true?
questions.explanation: If \(x>0\), then \(x^2>0\), so \(P\) is sufficient for \(Q\). However, \(x^2>0\) does not imply \(x>0\), because \(x=-1\) satisfies \(x^2>0\) but not \(x>0\). Therefore, \(Q\) is not sufficient for \(P\), and the true statement is option B.
questions.hint: Check whether each condition guarantees the other, and test negative values as possible counterexamples.
